prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean case of a new measurement capability that changed what physics can observe. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift of the trapping field, so many atoms can be interrogated at once in a Doppler- and recoil-free configuration. Ye's group, together with other strontium and ytterbium groups, took this to fractional uncertainties at or below 1e-18, with stability good enough to resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres. The same capability is now used for tests of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, relativistic geodesy and the planned redefinition of the second. The result is experimentally decisive rather than a proposal: independent clocks at several national laboratories and universities agree at the 1e-18 level, which is the kind of reproducibility I look for. Five of eight members rank it in their top three, and it is the only candidate that all eight members ranked at all. The two-name attribution is also the cleanest on the list, with the concept and first realization (Katori) and the performance frontier (Ye) mapping onto two people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlled single quantum systems (ion clocks and cavity QED) cover much of the enabling toolkit, so a lattice-clock prize could be read as an incremental extension of precision spectroscopy rather than a new discovery. A second reservation is that the headline application, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, and the strongest fundamental-physics payoffs (dark-matter limits, variation of constants) are so far null results that tighten bounds rather than reveal new phenomena. Finally, the allocation leaves out the many groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN, Tokyo and elsewhere who drove the Sr and Yb clocks to their current level, and I would want the citation to be worded so it does not imply the clock family has a single origin.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube discovery of astrophysical neutrinos first as a genuine clue from nature that opened a new observational window, and ranks the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube is a real discovery and a bold instrument, and I would not dismiss it: I keep it as an alternative. But where I differ is on ripeness of the attribution. The diffuse-flux observation rests on a collaboration of several hundred people and on AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND predecessors, so three names (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) will always look partly arbitrary, whereas the lattice-clock credit maps cleanly onto the concept and the record performance. I would also note that the lattice clock is itself a window onto gravity: millimetre-scale redshift measurements are a direct test of general relativity in a regime no other instrument reaches. Ulf, if the committee is troubled by the collaboration problem, would you accept a two-name IceCube prize (Halzen, Karle), as Olsson proposes, or does that leave out too much?

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first, regards Katori and Ye as a fair two-name credit, treats other groups as confirmation rather than missing laureates, and sees recognition as timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I largely agree, and as an atomic physicist she is well placed to judge the idea-versus-implementation split. I would add one qualification to her view that other groups are only confirmation. The magic-wavelength condition is the key idea, but the practical clock depended on the cold-atom engineering (cooling on narrow lines, lattice loading, spin polarization, and cavity-stabilized ultranarrow lasers) developed in several laboratories, so the effort was shared. That does not change my recommendation, but it argues for a citation worded around the lattice-clock concept and its realization. I would also ask her to check whether she sees any case for adding the many-body clock work as part of Ye's credit, since I think it is a real extension but not essential to the core claim.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as the clearest recent case of a quantitative flat-band prediction followed by decisive experiment, which opened moire quantum matter, and ranks the lattice clock only fifth.
responses.response: I take the theory-then-experiment argument seriously and Bistritzer and MacDonald's prediction is genuinely elegant. My disagreement is about maturity and about the experimental evidence. Eriksson himself notes that the nature of the superconducting pairing is unsettled, and from the experimental side I see strong sample-to-sample variation, twist-angle inhomogeneity and a field where independent groups still disagree about which phases are intrinsic. A prize now would credit three people for a field whose central open question is still unresolved, and the experimental credit is complicated by Yuan Cao and other junior authors and by parallel work from Dean, Young, Efetov and others. By comparison lattice clocks have been compared across continents for over a decade without a disputed interpretation. I would rank twisted graphene a few years later, not lower in scientific interest.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for its simple, general continuum model that is understood and not just observed, ranks topological insulators second, and ranks the lattice clock fourth with a clean idea followed by a spectacular precision realization.
responses.response: I agree with his description of the lattice clock as an unusually clear, original idea followed by a precision realization, and I appreciate that he treats the 2005 prize as a precedent rather than a bar. On his preference for B006, I accept the elegance of the model, but the committee has to ask what the prize would be for, and a field with an unresolved central mechanism is harder to describe in a short citation than a measurement that works. His second choice, topological insulators, faces the question of how much it adds beyond the 2016 prize and the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which he himself flags as a real attribution issue. I would sooner not have that problem on the table when a cleaner candidate exists.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a genuine invention that changed an entire instrument class and is overdue, and ranks the lattice clock fourth as an invention with demonstrated performance.
responses.response: Her argument is close to my own value system, since new instruments that let us see or measure what was previously out of reach are what I look for, and aberration correction clearly qualifies. I rank it lower mainly because only three members place it in their rankings at all, so it has a narrow base of support, and because Krivanek and Dellby's STEM correction is a credit-allocation problem she herself flags. On the other hand, I would take her point about long delay seriously: correctors have been commercial for two decades, so the argument that lattice clocks are too recent applies even less to her candidate. If the committee wants a prize for instrument development, I would be open to discussing B013 in a two-part configuration, but I would need a cleaner answer on how the three credited names relate to the STEM and TEM lines of correction.

uncertainties: Exact priority of the magic-wavelength lattice proposal relative to closely related proposals, and the weight to put on Ye's many-body strontium clock versus the original concept, is from memory and has not been verified here.
Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or as a continuation of precision spectroscopy.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a precondition for recognition or as supporting evidence that recognition is timely.

Whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with another measurement-driven discovery (IceCube or atom interferometry) would be preferable to a single clock prize, given the three-person limit and credit allocation problems in those candidates.
statement.conflict_note: No direct collaboration, institutional tie or financial link to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. One loose connection to flag: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA during my PhD, and Jun Ye is at JILA, so there is a shared scientific lineage and community, though the profile shows no joint work. I also lead quantum sensing activity within the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and member Johansson, and this would bear on B024 and B010 rather than on my preferred candidate, so I would consider recusal from those if they became prize candidates.
